whisper.label: Whisper Large-V3
whisper.text:
So every time you unlock your iPhone, there's 30,000 dots that go onto your face.
They're all in the near infrared, so you can't see them.
And then they reconstruct a 3D image based off of the distortion of those dots.
Very complex, very difficult, but then that means very expensive.
Human skin is actually very unique.
Even if you take something like...
As we have Bobby here, this can trick most of those systems out there.
But the polarization images of this is different than my skin.
Even though the first application we've looked at is for this secure biometrics,
the polarization information is also completely new in these devices.
It really provides a potential for an entirely new form of sensing,
entirely new applications to come out.
This week, Misha spoke with Rob Devlin, co-founder and CEO of MetaLens,
about how metasurfaces are transforming optics from bulky lens stacks
into flat, massive...
...to mass-producible semiconductor devices.
Devlin explains how controlling light at the nanoscale unlocks entirely new sensing capabilities,
from polarization imaging to secure face recognition
that can distinguish human skin from masks and spoofs.
We also talk about his journey from his work as a graduate student at Harvard
and what it takes to scale a lab breakthrough into millions of devices.
Please welcome Rob Devlin.
Everyone has known that diffractive optics can do really interesting things,
and there were...
...sort of theoretical surfaces that if you could collapse everything into a theoretical flat surface,
you could do really interesting things with light.
Really, metasurfaces are the best way to realize diffractive optics.
And then once you start making these nanostructures as small as we're making them,
and you're making them sub-wavelength, and you're able to control the geometry,
the dispersion of light through these materials, then you can start doing things that diffractive optics wouldn't even be able to do.
...that diffractive optics wouldn't even be able to do.
...that diffractive optics wouldn't even be able to do.
...that diffractive optics wouldn't even be able to do.
So you get a whole new degree of freedom in how you can control light.
And I think really from metasurfaces, the biggest innovation of metasurfaces has been
the ability to mass produce them in the semiconductor fabs.
So everyone's known DOEs are great and could do really interesting things,
but they never quite scaled as much as everyone would have hoped,
because always in the manufacturing you had to go to multi-levels or you still had some curvature.
...and you still had some curvature.
It's that shrinking it all, flattening it all down to a single surface,
and then making it really easy to mass produce in the semiconductor fabs that
is the real innovation, and that's what let us scale very quickly.
...and that's what let us scale very quickly.
Yeah, this is like a big transitioning from prototyping to mass production.
Did you learn what are the key ingredients or what helped to make this transition happen?
...to make this transition happen?
I think a couple of the biggest things was,
doing design for manufacturing.
So again, we're not just considering the nominal requirement.
Like, you go out, you try to make a device, and the customer will give you some requirement.
I want this much light to go over here and this much light to go over here,
and I need to have this much of the light that's shined on the device end up in those two spots.
That's the base spec.
You had to then go and say, okay, now in order to make this,
cost effective and actually work for consumer electronics,
I need to make it work for 10 million devices, and they all have to be within 5% of the base spec.
And so then realizing we had to take all of these complexities of manufacturing that will come in.
We're not making the one-off samples in the Harvard clean room anymore.
We had to take all of those design, or all of those manufacturing,
and then we had to take all of the manufacturing complexities,
the randomness in the manufacturing process,
and then come up with designs that were manufacturable,
meaning that we actually incorporate that into the design process,
into our design tools to make sure that the end device ends up having good yield.
That was probably the biggest thing that we learned as we were going and bringing up the mass production process,
was you couldn't just target the nominal anymore.
You had to target the spread that was required to get good yield.
And that's a very different mindset and mentality than when you're a PhD student.
You're looking to get that paper picture, the image for your paper.
Right.
And it's just, yeah, I think there was someone early on, I forget what company it was at,
but they had said, you know, any PhD student could go into the clean room and make one of our devices,
but it takes a company of 20, 40 people to go and make one.
And it's like, 10 million of those devices all working the same way.
Yeah. It's like scaling up.
Yeah.
Let me see.
Wow.
And I think this is actually one of the examples, right?
For your most recent...
Yeah. So this one is...
How is it made on the wafer's level?
So I think this one has about 9,000 meta surfaces on it.
And this is actually an especially interesting wafer for us,
because...
When we started out, everything that we were working on was replacing a set of optics in the stack.
So if you take STMicro Electronics, for example,
they had a module, they already had a set of optics there.
The main benefit of the meta surface was simplifying the optical stack.
So maybe going from something that required three or four lenses down to the one single meta surface.
And then it also...
In turn, improved performance and things like that.
So we're competing with this injection mold optics.
Yeah. And in some ways we were using and already using some of the capabilities of the meta surfaces
to do some new and unique things that you couldn't do with conventional optics.
But for the most part, it was the complexity, size, and cost reduction.
I see.
